analysis.one_liner: Extends the Export-Import Bank through 2021 and raises its taxpayer-backed lending authority to $200 billion.
analysis.headline: The Export-Import Bank reauthorization died in a House committee without a vote and without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The Export-Import Bank lends and guarantees financing to help foreign customers buy American exports. This bill would have extended the bank's charter through 2021 and raised its total lending, guarantee, and insurance authority from $100 billion to $200 billion a year, while adding some new requirements: public notice before big deals are approved, government reports on the risk the bank poses to taxpayers, a ban on financing companies tied to sanctioned Iran activity, and language urging more financing for renewable energy exports. The bill never left committee: it got no cosponsors, no hearing vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large U.S. exporters and their foreign buyers gain the most, since the bill extends the bank's charter through 2021 and raises its lending authority to $200 billion a year, locking in subsidized government-backed export financing. Banks that arrange the financing gain a continued fee stream, and renewable-energy and textile exporters gain from targeted attention in the bill. The transparency and Iran-sanctions provisions would modestly benefit taxpayers and oversight groups.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large exporters, foreign buyers, and banks

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Export-Import Bank's authority through September 30, 2021, and raises its total lending, guarantee, and insurance authority to $200 billion per year by fiscal 2015.
Requires public notice on the bank's website 14 days before board approval of any transaction over $100 million, identifying the buyer, supplier, and guarantor.
Directs the Comptroller General to report on the bank's financial position, the risk it poses to taxpayers, and its estimated effect on U.S. employment.
Prohibits bank financing for people or companies engaged in sanctionable activities with Iran, and urges the bank to expand financing for renewable energy exports.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. taxpayers bear the contingent cost: they stand behind the bank's guarantees, and the bill directs a government study of exactly that risk. Any losses on loans to foreign buyers ultimately land on the public, and the expanded $200 billion authority scales up that exposure. Small exporters that get little of the bank's support gain relatively little.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the bank's aggregate lending, guarantee, and insurance authority from $100 billion to $120 billion in fiscal 2012, climbing to $200 billion per year for fiscal 2015-2021 — a large expansion of taxpayer-backed exposure to foreign borrowers.

The bill itself directs the Comptroller General to study the risk the bank poses to American taxpayers and whether its fees and loss reserves properly reflect that risk — an acknowledgment that the true cost of the expanded lending was uncertain.

The bill's new public disclosure of large transactions carves out confidential and proprietary business information and anything that could 'jeopardize jobs' by helping competitors, which limits how much the public would actually learn about the deals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's oversight pieces were real: public pre-approval notices for deals over $100 million, a GAO audit of the risk the bank poses to taxpayers, and a ban on financing companies tied to sanctioned Iran activity [S2][S3]. But those safeguards sat alongside the bill's core purpose — doubling the bank's taxpayer-backed lending cap to $200 billion and extending it nine years, a program whose benefits flow mostly to a few large exporters and their foreign customers while taxpayers carry the downside risk [S2][S3]. Even the bill's own transparency rules let the bank withhold proprietary information and anything that could tip off foreign competitors, which limits how much the public would actually see [S3]. On balance, a narrow oversight improvement wrapped around a large expansion of subsidized export credit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no vote was ever taken.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the bill on May 7, 2012, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
On June 1, 2012, it was referred to the Subcommittee on International Monetary Policy and Trade, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the 112th Congress.
The bill never received a committee vote or a vote on the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers were spared the bill's expanded $200 billion lending cap, though large exporters lost little in practice because Congress separately reauthorized the bank that same year and the bank's subsidized financing continued.

for.name: Rep. Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks; it was referred to committee the same day.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, passed it to a subcommittee, and never reported the bill out for a vote.

against.name: Spencer Bachus
against.what_they_did: As committee chair during the 112th Congress, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one cosponsored the bill, so the record shows no partisan alignment in either direction.

industries.industry: Large U.S. exporters (aircraft, energy, heavy equipment)
industries.note: The bill would lock in the bank — the main U.S. government channel of subsidized export financing — through 2021 and grow its lending cap from $100 billion to $200 billion a year. The benefits of that financing flow heavily to a handful of the largest exporters and their foreign buyers, while taxpayers stand behind the guarantees.
The bill extends through 2021 the system in which banks arrange and earn fees on bank-guaranteed export financing, keeping a government-backed fee channel in place.
The bill urges the bank to expand financing for renewable energy and energy-efficiency exports year after year and to report barriers to doing so.
The bill adds a textile industry seat on the bank's advisory committee and requires an annual report on financing for textile and apparel exports used in global supply chains.
